This paper introduces QUICKAR, an automatic system that reformulates inquiries to include relevant concepts, leveraging crowdsourced data on how different users perceive questions and their associated concepts. By integrating these user insights with the semantic relationships between ideas, the system identifies the most effective candidate concepts to suggest. We validate QUICKAR through a real-world evaluation using a dataset of 1,000 questions and 10,000 concepts, comparing its performance against a baseline approach. Experimental results demonstrate that QUICKAR significantly outperforms the baseline in terms of recall, precision, and Mean Average Precision (MAP).

This study introduces a novel preconditioner for the multi-segment Darcy equations, which are frequently employed to model fluid flow across varying geological strata. The proposed approach is designed to be resilient to significant parameter variations, including permeability, porosity, and the interface geometry between adjacent layers. We demonstrate that the preconditioner's effectiveness is independent of the mesh discretization, the specific interface geometry connecting layers, and the physical parameters of the multi-segment system. Furthermore, the preconditioner is constructed to be symmetric, and we prove that its eigenvalues are confined to a specific, bounded interval.

This study tackles the task of generating abstractive summaries for unstructured online discussions. We introduce a novel framework that integrates discourse connections to structure discussions into a hierarchical tree, enabling a more accurate representation of conversational flow. By leveraging this tree structure, the method groups related utterances into thematic segments and synthesizes these groups into a comprehensive discussion summary. We evaluated our approach on the Discourse Representation Theory (DRT) style discourse structure task and a discussion summarization benchmark, achieving state-of-the-art results on both tasks.

The Cross Section Doppler Widening (SDX) phenomenon is a crucial diagnostic tool for measuring the bulk velocity of solar plasma. This study introduces a novel approach to forecasting SDX values by leveraging the physical characteristics of solar data. We developed a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINNs) model that integrates physical laws as constraints within the loss function, thereby enforcing physically consistent predictions. This methodology offers a substantial advantage over standard data-driven models, which often lack physical interpretability. We applied the PINN model to forecast SDX values for the cross sections of the sun's atmosphere, utilizing data from the Atmospheric Imaging Assembly (AIA) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). The results demonstrate that PINNs outperform conventional models in terms of prediction accuracy, achieving a 10% reduction in Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) and a 20% reduction in Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE). Furthermore, the model successfully forecasts SDX values for future time steps, with the PINN-enhanced approach yielding a 10% improvement in RMSE and 10% improvement in MAPE compared to standard models. These findings confirm that PINNs are highly effective for forecasting solar atmospheric dynamics.

This work introduces the notion of $n$-pre-Lie algebras and outlines a method for constructing them from $n$-Lie algebras. The resulting structure is shown to be a special case of the digraph of $n$-Lie algebras. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the cohomological properties of $n$-pre-Lie algebras are effectively modeled by the underlying $n$-Lie algebra.

Cell-free massive MIMO networks are poised to serve as the primary infrastructure for fifth-generation (5G) and subsequent wireless systems. These architectures are designed to deliver ubiquitous coverage and high-quality service (QoS) by utilizing a vast array of distributed access points (APs) that jointly serve numerous user equipments (UEs). Although APs are typically homogeneous, practical scenarios often involve heterogeneous configurations due to varying hardware capabilities, differing power supplies, and varied deployment locations. This paper introduces a framework for managing varied QoS levels within cell-free massive MIMO systems. We begin by deriving the necessary conditions for achieving a target QoS level, followed by the development of a joint optimization framework that addresses AP power allocation and user association. This approach ensures that specified QoS levels are met for every UE. Furthermore, we propose a low-complexity algorithm based on block coordinate descent to solve the resulting non-convex optimization problem. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method successfully attains the desired QoS for all UEs while minimizing total transmit power.

We demonstrate that the translation operators $T_\gamma$ within a generalized noncommutative setting of $\mathbb R^n$ converge to the identity operator as the displacements $\gamma$ vanish. This convergence holds for the $L^p$ spaces of Fuglede-Kahane and Folland-Stein types, alongside Connes' $L^p$ spaces, provided the convergence is verified through the corresponding $p$-forms.

We examine the microscopic origins of composition and short-range memory effects within sheared disordered systems. By analyzing the spatial organization of particles in a two-dimensional sheared granular assembly, we demonstrate that the short-term memory observed in the non-affine displacement field arises from the structural characteristics of the local particle neighborhood. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the dynamics of these neighborhoods and the concept of bond-orientational order, revealing that the link between composition and memory is mediated through the link between composition and bond-orientational order.

Object detection within the field of computer vision has garnered significant attention, with Ongoing Object Detection (OOD) emerging as a specialized subfield. OOD is defined as the task of identifying objects in a current video frame by leveraging detections from preceding frames. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of OOD, beginning with its fundamental concepts and specific application domains. The article further outlines the core challenges inherent to OOD and examines the most effective existing methodologies. Finally, the survey concludes by identifying key obstacles in OOD research and suggests potential avenues for future development.

We introduce a modification to the $g\to c\bar{c}$ splitting function within the BDMPS-Z framework, accounting for the medium's influence on the initial-state radiation emitted by a heavy quark-antiquark pair. This adjustment is derived by calculating the emission spectrum of soft photons from the heavy quark in a medium, which is then compared to the vacuum spectrum. Our analysis reveals that the medium significantly suppresses the splitting function, particularly for hard gluons.

This study introduces a novel, interpretable domain generalization (DG) approach for image classification that leverages domain-agnostic latent representations. By utilizing a pre-trained model, we first derive these domain-invariant features and subsequently employ a specialized classifier to perform recognition. The method's interpretability stems from its utilization of saliency maps generated via Integrated Gradients to analyze the significance of specific image regions. These visual insights facilitate the manual selection of representative samples from the source domains, which are then used to train a classifier capable of generalizing to unseen target domains. Experimental results on standard DG benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves performance on par with current state-of-the-art methods.

This paper introduces a new framework designed to improve security and awareness for IoT devices, autonomous vehicles, and drones. This framework utilizes a decentralized blockchain to facilitate inter-agent communication, ensuring that only verified agents can access the network. This approach guarantees that the blockchain remains free of malicious actors, thereby bolstering overall network security. $\alpha$-attractor models are a prominent category of inflationary theories that encompass numerous models within the supergravity framework. This study introduces a novel inflationary paradigm, termed the $\alpha$-attractor expansion, which is derived from the Kaluza-Klein reduction of higher-dimensional gravity. We demonstrate that this expansion approach yields the same inflationary predictions as the $\alpha$-attractor models. Furthermore, we examine the specific case of $\alpha$-attractor expansion within the context of the Swampland conjectures.

Machine learning (ML) has become ubiquitous across numerous sectors, including healthcare, finance, and transportation. While the demand for ML has surged, the hardware infrastructure supporting it has not kept pace, resulting in significant bottlenecks. To address this, Intel has introduced the Intel Data Center Accelerator Platform (DCAP), which offers a suite of optimizations for accelerating ML workloads on Intel Xeon processors. This paper details our findings from evaluating the DCAP platform's impact on end-to-end ML frameworks, specifically examining the benefits of various optimizations. We also present a comprehensive performance analysis of the platform's effects on the PyTorch framework, covering both training and inference phases. Our results indicate that the PyTorch framework can achieve up to 1.7x speedup in training and up to 1.5x speedup in inference when utilizing the DCAP platform.

In Bayesian statistics, the Bayes factor (BF) is widely used to evaluate the null hypothesis, yet it is susceptible to misinterpretation. To address this, Linde et al. (2021) proposed a method for calculating the Bayes factor from a credible interval, which is equivalent to the highest density interval (HDI) and the region of practical equivalence (ROPE). The present study replicates this approach and demonstrates that the procedure effectively reverses the conventional algorithm originally formulated by Kruschke (2013). In Kruschke's framework, the ROPE is established first, followed by the generation of a posterior distribution that satisfies the specified equivalence constraints; the resulting HDI is then computed, and the BF is derived from the overlap between the HDI and the ROPE. Our replication confirms that Linde et al.'s method can accurately reconstruct the BF from these parameters. Furthermore, we illustrate that the bidirectional relationship between the Bayes factor and the HDI/ROPE overlap allows for the derivation of these metrics from one another.

This study introduces a novel vector-quantized semantic communication framework, which diverges from conventional methods by transmitting the codebook along with the message. This approach allows the receiver to reconstruct the intended message with higher accuracy. The system's performance is evaluated using mean squared error (MSE) and an objective metric named the semantic similarity score (sss). Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior MSE performance and offers greater flexibility compared to traditional systems.

The surge in data volume, variety, and velocity has driven the widespread adoption of big data analytics across numerous sectors. Nevertheless, the inherent complexity of these datasets, combined with the diverse needs of end-users, creates significant hurdles for organizations aiming to derive actionable insights. This paper introduces a new framework designed to facilitate user interaction with massive data through a three-layered architecture. The first layer, a data ingestion and processing component, manages the acquisition, cleaning, and preparation of data from varied sources. The second layer comprises a data analytics component that delivers a broad spectrum of analytical methods, ranging from traditional data mining and machine learning to advanced AI and deep learning. The third layer, a data visualization component, presents analytical results through interactive, user-friendly interfaces. This modular design enables users to engage with and interrogate large-scale data sets, allowing them to refine analytical approaches and explore multiple perspectives. Furthermore, the framework is equipped to handle data in real-time, facilitating the immediate delivery of actionable insights.

Time-varying networks are increasingly common in various domains, including finance, epidemiology, and economics. While Time Autoregression (TAR) models have been widely adopted to capture temporal dependencies, they often fail to account for dynamic network structures. Conversely, Visual Helper Clustered Network Autoregression (VHCNAR) models have emerged as a leading solution for time series data with evolving networks. However, these models typically rely on a fixed number of clusters, which restricts their ability to accurately capture complex temporal dynamics. To address this, we introduce the Visual Helper Clustered Network Autoregression (VHCNAR) framework enhanced with a nonparametric Bayesian approach. This new method allows for flexible, data-driven determination of the number of clusters. Empirical evaluations using both simulated datasets and real-world data demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in modeling time series with time-varying networks.

The task of verifying academic claims involves determining whether a claim's truthfulness based on supporting or contradictory evidence. While retrieval-based approaches have emerged as a promising solution by utilizing semantic similarity to locate relevant evidence, they often suffer from underperforming due to the retrieval of irrelevant or redundant information. This study proposes a straightforward yet effective method to mitigate retrieval issues by diminishing the representation of non-critical evidence within the classifier. Our findings demonstrate that this strategy significantly boosts performance across three distinct datasets.

Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is a non-invasive imaging technique capable of generating high-resolution, three-dimensional representations of the human eye. This study introduces a novel deep learning framework designed to automatically segment the posterior segment of the eye using OCT data. The proposed method comprises two primary components: a multi-scale segmentation network for isolating the posterior ocular segment and a retrieval network for localizing specific regions of interest within the OCT volume. Experimental results demonstrate that the segmentation network achieves a Dice coefficient of 0.94, while the retrieval network attains a mean Average Precision (mAP) of 0.89. These findings indicate that the framework can effectively and accurately identify the posterior segment of the eye from OCT images, thereby facilitating the automated analysis of specific anatomical structures.

Superstatistics serves as a statistical modeling framework designed to handle data characterized by fluctuating temperatures and non-Gaussian distributions. This study introduces a neural superstatistics model, which applies this framework to neural data to account for fluctuating cognitive states. We employ a Bayesian inference approach to estimate the parameters of this model from neural recordings. The proposed method is validated using both simulated and actual electrophysiological data. Furthermore, the model's performance is benchmarked against standard Superstatistics and other established statistical models. Our findings indicate that the neural superstatistics model effectively captures the underlying characteristics of fluctuating cognitive states.

We examine the excitation of the C{1} hyperfine transitions in molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies, specifically focusing on the effects of subthermal excitation. This phenomenon arises from the interaction between the C{1} ground state and the excited hyperfine levels of the C{1} molecule, driven by the low-energy collisions with the H{1} ground state. We demonstrate that this subthermal excitation can significantly alter the C{1} line ratios and intensities, potentially distorting the derived physical properties of the gas. We further show that the C{1} line ratios are highly sensitive to the H{1} number density, making them a useful diagnostic tool for probing the physical conditions of the gas. We also discuss the implications of our findings for the interpretation of the C{1} line ratios in the context of the molecular gas reservoirs of galaxies.

Code-switching involves alternating between two languages within a single utterance, a phenomenon that has garnered significant attention from linguists and researchers. This study presents the inaugural treebank dedicated to Verbal Frisian-Dutch code-mixing, utilizing a corpus of 1,000 sentences. We outline the specific linguistic characteristics of this code-mixing, detail the rigorous annotation protocol, and provide illustrative examples. Furthermore, we demonstrate the corpus's potential by employing it to train a transformer model capable of predicting the annotated linguistic categories.

This study investigates the influence of stellar mass on photoevaporation within protoplanetary disks. We utilize a 1D hydrodynamic model to simulate the evolution of the outer disk regions, incorporating realistic stellar X-ray and UV emission spectra. Our findings indicate that disks around low-mass stars (M < 0.8 M☉) are subject to more intense photoevaporation than those around high-mass stars (M > 0.8 M☉). Consequently, low-mass star systems lose their gaseous disks more slowly, extending the duration of the gas phase and allowing a greater variety of planet types to form. Furthermore, the outer disk evolution of these low-mass star systems is primarily driven by soft X-rays, whereas high-mass star systems are dominated by hard X-rays.

This study introduces a novel, explicit high-order generalized-$\alpha$ method for structural dynamics, designed to be integrated with isogeometric analysis (IGA). The proposed technique is capable of modeling both linear and nonlinear behaviors, including both elastic and plastic responses. The method's accuracy and stability are validated through numerical tests involving spatially and temporally smooth solutions, as well as those exhibiting discontinuities. The results demonstrate that the new method surpasses the standard low-order approach in terms of accuracy, particularly when utilizing high-order NURBS-based IGAs.

The Bose polaron, representing a dressed impurity within a weakly interacting Bose gas, serves as a model for investigating impurity-particle interactions in diverse quantum systems. This study employs a one-dimensional twin-well setup to analyze the decay of polaronic residues following impurity removal. We demonstrate that this residual population can be significantly reduced by adjusting the double-well potential to trigger either intra- or interband excitations. Furthermore, we examine the spatial distribution of the remaining impurity and its associated cloud, as well as the influence of potential ramping speeds on decay processes. These findings offer valuable insights into the dynamics of the Bose polaron and pave the way for future investigations into its decay mechanisms.

This study addresses the logistical challenge of distributing aid to disaster victims, a task complicated by the unpredictable nature of the events themselves. We introduce a multi-phase approach to modeling this problem, where each phase represents a distinct operational stage. To tackle the uncertainty inherent in these scenarios, we develop and apply stochastic optimization methods, specifically two-point robustness and scenario-based planning. Our methodology is validated through case studies involving earthquake and flood disasters, with results demonstrating that the multi-phase stochastic optimization framework effectively supports aid distribution planning.

Pulsar timing arrays (PTAs) are currently detecting the nanohertz gravitational wave background (GWB) generated by a population of supermassive black hole binaries (SMBHBs). While the standard assumption is that these systems are circular, observational evidence suggests SMBHBs often retain significant orbital eccentricity. To accurately model these eccentric signals, we have developed a highly precise, computationally efficient, and publicly accessible numerical tool for generating PTA waveforms. This implementation utilizes a perturbative approach based on the post-Newtonian (PN) expansion to calculate eccentricity-driven signal deviations. Our method achieves a relative error below $10^{-3}$ for PN orders up to 11, with an additional $O(\text{PN} 12)$ term estimated to maintain a relative error under $10^{-2}$. Our analysis reveals that SMBHB eccentricity induces detectable modulations in the PTA Hellings-Readington correlation function, with the magnitude of these modulations scaling with the eccentricity and the ratio of the source's orbital period to that of the PTAs. Furthermore, we evaluated the computational costs of waveform generation across various post-Newtonian orders and explored strategies to enhance performance.

This paper introduces a novel method for analyzing activities within worldwide programming contests. We developed a novel metric called "difficulty" to evaluate the complexity of individual problems. By applying this to specific tasks, we examined how the chosen difficulty metric correlates with solving rates, revealing a clear positive link between difficulty and submission volume. Our analysis also uncovered a previously unidentified phenomenon: the "solving cliff," characterized by a sudden drop in solved rates as task difficulty rises. Furthermore, we investigated the relationship between solving rates and the time limit allocated for each problem.

This study introduces a novel on-chip methodology for analyzing high-viscosity liquids at millimeter-wave frequencies, specifically within the 750 GHz to 1100 GHz range. The approach utilizes a coplanar waveguide (CPW) featuring a microfluidic channel, where the liquid flows through a channel etched into the substrate beneath the CPW. The liquid's viscosity is determined by measuring the channel's pressure drop in response to varying flow rates. The paper details the design and fabrication of a 940 GHz test structure, presents experimental results validating the method, and outlines a roadmap for future development.

The global COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant devastation, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to issue guidelines for managing the virus. This paper introduces a framework designed to aid in the management of the disease by leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) and multi-source data analysis. The proposed system comprises three primary components: (1) a data collection module utilizing various sensors and sensors to gather data from diverse sources, including smartphones, wearable devices, and environmental monitors; (2) an AI-based data analysis module that employs machine learning algorithms to detect patterns and predict outbreaks; and (3) an action-oriented module that generates actionable recommendations based on the analysis results. This paper provides an overview of the proposed framework, discusses its potential applications, and outlines future research directions.

This paper introduces a multi-scale Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) framework designed to address multi-phase fluid-structure interaction problems. The approach employs a hybrid method that combines a standard SPH formulation for the fluid domain with a meshless version of the Discrete Element Method (DEM) for the dispersed phase. To model interactions between the phases, a modified version of the Drinfeld et al. SPH-DEM scheme is utilized. Additionally, the fluid-structure interaction scheme described in Zhang et al. (2019) is integrated to couple the SPH fluid with a boundary element method (BEM) for the structure. The hybrid SPH-DEM scheme and the fluid-structure scheme are linked through a coupling mechanism that transfers forces from the dispersed phase to the solid boundary. The efficacy of this proposed framework is demonstrated via simulations of a wave tank experiment involving a floating breakwater and a single spherical particle. The results align well with experimental data, and the method's versatility is further illustrated by applying it to a case involving a floating breakwater and multiple particles.

Nodal surfaces in momentum space (NMSs) represent a topologically protected, three-dimensional region within the Brillouin zone where the dispersion curve intersects the energy level set to zero. These structures have garnered significant attention due to their capacity to host unique topological phenomena, such as the Weyl point, as well as the nodal-line and nodal-surface classifications. In this review, we examine the topological attributes of NMSs and explore their application in photonic systems, highlighting recent advancements in their experimental realization. Furthermore, we extend the discussion to other physical contexts where NMSs have been observed, including cold atoms, ultracold fermions, and magnons.

This work establishes the invariance of partial averaging operators within holomorphically transitive actions on real analytic manifolds, specifically for instances involving finite groups. Additionally, we demonstrate an application regarding the spectral properties of averages defined on unimodular lattices within $\mathrm{SL}(n,\mathbb{R})$.

This study presents the first observational confirmation of a dense disk of dark molecular matter in the outer regions of the Milky Way. By analyzing the 12CO J=1-0 emission line, we identified a substantial molecular disk extending from approximately 10 to 20 kiloparsecs from the Galactic center. This structure is characterized by a high mass-to-light ratio of 100–1000 M$_\odot$/L$_\odot$, indicating that dark matter dominates its mass budget. The existence of this disk implies that dark matter possesses a non-zero velocity dispersion, with a lower limit of 100 km/s. Furthermore, the observed CO emission is consistent with a molecular gas density of roughly 10$^{-3}$ M$_\odot$/pc$^3$ and a velocity dispersion of 10 km/s. We propose that this outer disk consists of molecular gas trapped within a dark matter halo, which has been isolated from the inner galaxy by the Milky Way's bar. This trapped gas has likely been enriched with heavy elements over time, resulting in a metallicity of approximately 0.1 Z$_\odot$.

This paper presents a restricted economic framework where the supply of services is fixed, independent of compensation, and explores the resulting market equilibrium. By examining a model economy with these constraints, the study investigates how labor compensation shifts affect service demand and the equilibrium price level. The findings indicate that reducing wages results in a rise in service prices, conversely, a continuous increase in wages leads to a decrease in their corresponding pricing levels.

We investigate the collective behavior of polar active matter characterized by significant disorder and particle thickness, utilizing a two-dimensional model with disordered motility and interactions. This framework incorporates both steric forces and hydrodynamic interactions, with motility disorder arising from spatial fluctuations in motility persistence. We examine how this disorder influences active force alignment, local ordering, and large-scale dynamics. Our findings reveal that thick disordered systems exhibit a distinct dynamical regime where hydrodynamic interactions drive the formation of large-scale vortices, even in the absence of alignment-favoring conditions. We further demonstrate that increasing disorder in motility suppresses large-scale polarization, resulting in a novel state of active turbulence.

This study explores the challenge of determining an agent's location within a scene through dialogue with human observers. We introduce a corpus comprising 1000 video clips, each featuring a human and an embodiment agent positioned at distinct points. We generate scripted dialogues between these parties using a predefined set of templates, where the human describes their own position relative to the agent. We then evaluate two automated methods for generating descriptions based on the current scene layout and assess their performance in training a speaker to infer the agent's location from these utterances. Our findings indicate that a speaker generating descriptions by observing the human's actual position outperforms an agent that infers the human's position solely from its own physical stance.

Vibration analysis is a widely used technique for monitoring rotating equipment, where the selection of appropriate frequency bands is critical for accurate fault diagnosis. However, manually choosing these bands is often time-consuming and prone to errors. To address this, a novel automatic frequency band selection method called Band Significance Factor (BSF) is proposed. BSF integrates the Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) with a new metric, the Band Significance Factor (BSF), to evaluate each band's importance. The process involves calculating the BSF for every band and then aggregating these values to determine the optimal band. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through two case studies involving vibration data from a ball bearing and a gear. Results indicate that BSF outperforms existing techniques in both selecting the best frequency bands and classifying the condition of the components.

We present muon-spin relaxation (muSR) findings regarding the superconducting ground states of the noncentrosymmetric compounds CaIrSi3 and CaPtSi3. These materials exhibit superconducting transition temperatures of 4.5 K and 4.0 K, respectively. Our results indicate that both compounds display isotropic superconducting behaviors, characterized by the absence of nodes and a lack of anisotropy. These observations align with the theoretical expectations for a triplet superconducting state.

This study introduces a novel methodology for the optimal control of stochastic systems, specifically addressing the challenge of solving the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation. The approach employs a sparse grid framework to approximate the HJB solution, utilizing gradient descent to iteratively refine the costate function. The performance of this method is validated through a case study on a stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) control problem, where the objective is to determine an optimal control policy for a linear system subject to random disturbances. The findings demonstrate that the proposed methodology effectively mitigates the curse of dimensionality, offering a promising avenue for solving HJB equations in high-dimensional optimal control scenarios.

Quantum computing is poised to outperform classical systems in specific domains, such as machine learning, cryptography, and quantum simulation. This study introduces a novel quantum classification framework that leverages the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) state to categorize $N$-qubit strings into odd or even classes. The proposed method utilizes Hadamard transformations and CNOT gates to generate an $N$-qubit GHZ state, followed by a CNOT operation with an auxiliary qubit to execute the logical XOR operation on the input data. Our analysis demonstrates that this approach is both feasible and scalable.

This study employs rapid magnetic resonance imaging (RMI) to track heat distribution within a gas-solid stationary bed. The experimental setup involved a gas flowing through a packed bed of particles contained within a 30 mm diameter cylinder, which was placed inside an MRI scanner. The bed was heated from the top by a 100 W electric heater, with temperature data collected from the MRI images at a spatial resolution of 0.5 mm and a temporal resolution of 10 seconds. The gas velocity was varied between 0.01 and 0.05 m/s, while the inlet temperature ranged from 20 to 40°C. The results indicate that the average temperature of the particles is directly proportional to the inlet temperature and the heating power, but decreases as gas velocity increases. Furthermore, the temperature distribution across the bed is non-uniform, with the highest temperatures observed at the top and the lowest at the bottom.

We introduce a theoretical framework for superconductivity in UTe$_2$ that integrates thermal fluctuations with disorder. This approach accounts for the experimentally observed reentrant superconductivity, suggesting that disorder acts as the primary driver of this phenomenon. Specifically, our model indicates that applying mild pressure to UTe$_2$ with low concentrations of defects should enhance its superconducting critical temperature.

Ultra-wideband (UWB) technology is a radio standard designed for transmitting data packets over a wide frequency spectrum. While the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has mandated UWB for various applications, including radar and medical devices, it has not yet specified a particular UWB physical layer (PHY) configuration. Consequently, this study proposes a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) framework to automatically determine the optimal UWB PHY settings in real-time. The primary goal is to maximize the average data rate by selecting the ideal modulation scheme, frequency band, and pulse shape. The proposed DRL agent is trained using a simulator that models the wireless channel and the specific PHY characteristics. The agent learns to select the best configuration by observing the resulting data rate and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). The effectiveness of this approach is validated through simulations, which demonstrate that the DRL agent successfully converges to an optimal policy that maximizes the average data rate.

This study examines the k-median grouping problem within the context of discrete Fr\'eche t and Hausdorff metrics. We establish that the problem is NP-hard for both metrics, while also developing a 2-approximation algorithm specifically for the discrete Fr\'e chet metric.

Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has emerged as a promising approach for addressing complex, large-scale optimization problems. However, the inherent non-stationarity of MARL algorithms, driven by the dynamic learning behaviors of other agents, poses significant challenges to their stability and convergence. This paper introduces a novel MARL framework that integrates the minimax game-theoretic model with double averaging techniques to achieve robust convergence. By employing the minimax setting, the method ensures that the policy gradient aligns with the direction of the optimal solution. Furthermore, the double averaging technique is utilized to mitigate the impact of stochasticity in the algorithm. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the method achieves a convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the average regret, where $T$ represents the number of iterations. Numerical experiments on the classic multi-robot coordination problem validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

This paper examines the verification of temporal properties within systems modeled by coalgebras. Specifically, we analyze coalgebraic validity across languages from the family of arithmetic $\mu$-calculi, which extend standard branching time $\mu$-calculi with arithmetic predicates. We introduce a coalgebraic framework for these calculies, where each operator corresponds to a functor. We demonstrate that, provided the functor is accessible, the associated validity operator admits a dual form. We establish that this duality holds for all arithmetic $\mu$-calculi, and further show that the resulting bisimulations are both right and final. Finally, we apply these findings to develop a sound and complete coalgebraic semantics for the fragment of the arithmetic $\mu$-calculies that support the modal $\mu$-calculus with unary fixed points.

This study introduces a new approach for inferring unknown initial states in partial differential equations (PDEs) by leveraging observed data at specific times. The method employs a low-rank tensor framework to address the associated optimization challenge, which is formulated as a nonsmooth, non-convex problem due to the non-linear nature of the PDE solution map. To resolve this, we develop an efficient algorithm that combines the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) with the Smooth Approximation of the ReLU function. The efficacy of the proposed technique is validated through numerical experiments on two test cases: the linear advection equation and the non-linear Burgers equation.

This study introduces a drive-through air quality monitoring system that employs a regenerative facility location algorithm to determine optimal sensor placement. The system integrates a vehicle-mounted air quality monitor with a GPS unit, a setup previously validated in our prior research. The proposed air quality chart utilizes this algorithm to identify the ideal locations for sampling. The research evaluates the efficacy of using GPS to select these sampling points and compares the resulting charts against those generated by a Chordal Distance algorithm. The findings indicate that the GPS-based approach offers superior performance, as it effectively minimizes the number of drive-throughs required to create an accurate and comprehensive air quality map.

Let $R$ denote a finite ring of truncated polynomials over a finite field $q$, possessing an involutory operation $\tilde{}$ that distinguishes two classes of elements. We define $G$ as the general linear group of $R$-modules and utilize the associated skew-associative polynomial $\text{tr}(x \tilde{}) x$ to construct Weil representations of $G$ on a free $R$-module of finite dimension. This work establishes two foundational results: the decomposition of Weil representations over $R$ into sums of representations over specific subrings $R_1$ and $R_2$, and the decomposition of the Weil representation of $G$ into components involving the general linear groups of $R$ that stabilize specific one-dimensional subspaces.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has sparked significant interest in automatically generating videos, a field that has garnered substantial attention from both researchers and industry practitioners. This surge in focus stems from the widespread adoption of social media platforms, which have become integral to daily life. These channels serve as vital tools for disseminating information, promoting products, and persuading audiences. Consequently, there is a growing demand for automated video creation to support marketing campaigns and brand promotion. This paper reviews the state-of-the-art techniques in AI-driven convincing video generation, examining how various methods leverage facial expressions, body language, and voice synthesis to produce lifelike digital avatars. We critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of current approaches, discuss emerging challenges, and propose potential future research directions.

This study examines quantum squeezing within the dynamics of ions held by quadrupole and octopole ion traps. We derive the Hamiltonian for the system and identify the corresponding squeezed coherent states of motion. Furthermore, we calculate the quantum fluctuations of the relevant state variables and evaluate the degree of nonclassicality through the squeezing parameter. Our findings demonstrate that these quantum states exhibit significant squeezing, indicating that the ion's motion in these configurations is substantially nonclassical.

Neuroscience frameworks are increasingly employed to investigate the origins of cognition and behavior, with the aim of advancing artificial intelligence. However, the intricate nature of these models renders them difficult to manage, as they require the optimization of numerous hyper-parameters. Consequently, this study introduces a machine learning strategy to forecast optimal hyper-parameters for neuroscience frameworks. The research utilizes a dataset comprising 1,000 simulations of the spiking neural network (SNN) architecture, which is a common model in neuroscience. By applying a deep learning approach to this data, the authors achieved a prediction accuracy of 90%.

Camouflaged object segmentation (COS) is a difficult computer vision challenge because blending with the background makes these objects nearly invisible. This issue is particularly prevalent in real-world scenarios, such as surveillance and search-and-rescue missions, where detecting hidden targets is critical. To address this, we introduce a new large-scale dataset comprising 1,000 images of camouflaged objects. The dataset includes three distinct categories: camouflaged animals, insects, and furniture. To further support research, we have developed a robust benchmarking framework that evaluates various state-of-the-art methods using multiple metrics, including the F-score, Cam, and Feature-level Distance metrics. Additionally, we have proposed a new technique that integrates the advantages of both supervised and unsupervised approaches, achieving superior performance on our benchmark. We have also made the dataset and benchmarking framework publicly available to encourage further research in this field.

This study examines how Lorentz violation influences superconductivity by modifying the standard BCS framework to include a term derived from the Standard Model Extension (SME). Specifically, we analyze a CPT-odd dimension-three operator within the fermion kinetic energy that couples to the background vector $\bar{n}^\mu$. Our analysis reveals that this background field breaks galilean invariance in the superconducting state, causing the order parameter to acquire dependence on the laboratory frame. Furthermore, we investigate how these effects alter the critical temperature and the energy gap, demonstrating that the dimension-three operator induces anisotropy in the energy gap.

AI systems are increasingly integrated into critical decision-making processes, yet their opacity and susceptibility to errors remain significant concerns. This study investigates how crowdsourced reporting facilitates the detection of AI mistakes. We conducted a user study involving 1,000 participants across 10 countries, asking them to identify errors in two AI systems: one for detecting COVID-19 cases and another for identifying COVID-19-related news. Participants were instructed to submit findings via a dedicated online interface, which included a crowdsourced reporting feature. The results indicate that this reporting mechanism substantially enhanced the volume and quality of crowd submissions, enabling the identification of 1,000 defects in the COVID news classifier and 1,000 in the COVID case detector. Furthermore, a crowdsourced reporting feature significantly improved the volume and quality of crowd submissions, enabling the identification of 1,000 defects in the COVID news classifier and 1,000 in the COVID case detector. Additionally, participants were asked to verify the accuracy of these reports, with verification rates reaching 90% for the news classifier and 80% for the COVID case detector. Finally, we developed a novel method to generate synthetic explanations for AI errors, allowing users to understand the underlying causes of these mistakes.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in object recognition, yet their inherent sequential processing limits inference speed. To address this bottleneck, we introduce R(Det)^2, a sequential routing framework that enhances both processing efficiency and accuracy. The system operates by dividing the input image into multiple regions, each processed by a dedicated neural network. These networks are trained using a stochastic routing mechanism that generates diverse detection hypotheses, which are subsequently refined by a second-stage detector. Experimental results indicate that R(Det)^2 surpasses existing methods in object detection accuracy, achieving gains of 1.4% and 0.7% over the VGG16 baseline on the PASCAL VOC 2012 and COCO datasets, respectively. Furthermore, the framework delivers a significant reduction in computational cost, improving efficiency by a factor of 2.5x compared to VGG16.

Adversarial training is a critical technique for enhancing the robustness of deep neural networks, yet it is computationally demanding and often yields only marginal improvements in accuracy. A primary factor contributing to these limitations is catastrophic overfitting, a phenomenon where the model learns to fit noise within the adversarially generated examples. This study introduces a new method, ZeroGrad, which effectively mitigates catastrophic overfitting by enforcing a zero gradient constraint on the clean example during adversarial generation. Theoretically, the method is grounded in the concept of zero curvature, which ensures the generated adversarial example remains robust against its own perturbations. Empirical evaluations on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets demonstrate that ZeroGrad outperforms existing adversarial training approaches, achieving superior robustness without sacrificing accuracy.

This study examines the Thakurta metric, a black hole solution within the framework of $f(R,T)$ gravity, to determine if it accurately represents astrophysical black holes. We demonstrate that the Thakurta metric is merely a spherically symmetric solution for a perfect fluid, not a black hole solution, and therefore cannot describe astrophysical black holes. Consequently, recent claims asserting that limits on primordial black holes (PBHs) derived from the accretion of gas onto Thakurta black holes are flawed. We instead derive new constraints on PBHs using data from gravitational wave events detected by LIGO and Virgo. Our analysis indicates that PBHs with masses between $10^{23}$ and $10^{25}$ kg are effectively ruled out.

This study examines how persistent asset changes influence a specific category of hybrid-inspired optimization techniques. The proposed approach involves creating a specialized variant of differential evolution, which we term the "persistent differential evolution" (pDE). This method integrates a specific mechanism designed to retain solutions that have persisted for extended durations. We evaluate this new approach against the original differential evolution algorithm using the CEC 2017 benchmark suite, which includes both dynamic and static test functions. Our findings indicate that pDE consistently surpasses the original differential evolution in terms of performance.

Bootstrapping represents a critical challenge in fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), a field that has garnered significant attention in recent years. This work introduces a novel, bootstrappable scheme called BTS, which is built upon the BGV encryption framework and leverages ideal lattices. The BTS scheme offers two primary advantages: first, it employs a more straightforward bootstrapping procedure than prior BGV-based methods, and second, it achieves superior performance by utilizing a modulus set that is a power of 2. The core of the bootstrapping process involves the BTS-RLWE algorithm, which transforms the ciphertext into a ring learning with errors (RLWE) form. Subsequently, the BGV decryption routine is applied to convert this ciphertext back into the BGV format. The authors demonstrate that the scheme's security is derived from the hardness of the Ring-SIS and Ring-LWE problems. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the scheme's performance, including bootstrapping overhead, and includes experimental results to validate these findings.

This work examines a system of random matrices influenced by a double potential: one uniform across all matrices and another specific to each individual matrix. The uniform component accounts for interactions between matrices, while the distinct potential introduces self-interaction for each matrix. We analyze the scenario where the self-potential scales inversely with matrix dimension, effectively nullifying the matrices' own contributions in the large-d limit. We identify a specific logarithmic form for this scaling potential that permits exact solution via orthogonal polynomials. The resulting model features a unique family of five-point correlation functions, which can be expressed as integrals over the joint eigenvalue distributions of the matrix collection. These correlations are further characterized by universal behavior, linking the model to the large-d limit of matrix models defined on two-dimensional quantum gravity.

This study introduces a method for experimentally investigating quantum correlations within two-qutrit systems, utilizing polarization measurements on a pair of $^{39}$K atoms trapped in an optical dipole trap. We establish a generalized Bell-type inequality designed specifically for these highly dimensional systems and validate its efficacy through numerical simulations. Furthermore, we outline a feasible experimental protocol to test this inequality using $^{39}$K, where the magnetic spin components ($J_z$) of the two qutrits serve as the local observables.

We present a theorem establishing that within quantum theory, the condition of locality alone is insufficient to derive classical-like correlations; it must be paired with a distinct, non-trivial decomposability assumption to do so. This finding demonstrates that while quantum theory inherently violates this decomposability principle, it remains compatible with quantum relativity. Consequently, our result offers a new perspective compared to Bell's theorem by isolating the violation of decomposability rather than locality as the source of non-classical behavior.

StyleGAN2 has established itself as a leading image synthesis model, producing high-quality results that are difficult to distinguish from real images. However, it is limited to generating images only. In contrast, StyleGAN2-XL extends the framework to create high-fidelity portraits at resolutions up to 2K. This paper introduces StyleGAN-V, a novel approach to video generation that builds upon StyleGAN2 and StyleGAN2-XL. By utilizing a single set of parameters, StyleGAN-V generates videos of arbitrary length at resolutions of 1080p and higher, while maintaining quality comparable to image generation. The system employs a new loss function to ensure temporal consistency, which is crucial for video production. We demonstrate that StyleGAN-V can be trained on a single GPU using a dataset of 10,000 images and 100 hours of video, resulting in a model that is significantly more efficient than current state-of-the-art alternatives. Furthermore, the generated videos exhibit superior temporal coherence and quality compared to existing methods.

Accurate estimation of the exposure date is a critical step in reconstructing the radiation history of objects, such as archaeological artifacts. This dating process relies on the principle that trapped electrons in a material's crystal lattice gradually migrate to defects over time, resulting in a progressive decline in thermoluminescence (TL) signal intensity. Consequently, the residual TL signal serves as a proxy for the age of exposure. While traditional methods typically involve measuring a single TL signal, recent advancements have introduced techniques that utilize the entire TL signal spectrum. This study evaluates the efficacy of deep learning algorithms in estimating the exposure date from full TL signals. The results demonstrate that deep learning models achieve superior accuracy compared to conventional approaches, thereby offering a more robust and precise method for dating based on TL signal analysis.

This paper investigates an elliptic problem characterized by a double phase with a singular nonhomogeneous term, set on a complete manifold. The problem is defined by the differential equation $-\Delta u + V(x)u = \frac{f(x)}{|u|^\gamma} + g(x,u)$, subject to the Dirichlet boundary condition $u=0$ on the boundary $\partial\Omega$. Here, $V$ and $f$ are strictly positive functions, while $\gamma$ is a positive constant. The analysis assumes that the growth exponents for $g$ are unbalanced and exhibit a singularity. By applying the direct method of the mountain pass, we establish the existence of a classical positive solution. Additionally, we demonstrate the existence of a nontrivial nonnegative solution for a related case where the term $V(x)u$ is absent.

The Fastcat system, designed for rapid and compact cone beam CT (CBCT) imaging, offers a cost-effective and user-friendly solution for radiation therapy. This study validates the Fastcat's CT emulator by comparing its output with measurements from an Ionization Chamber and a CT water phantom. The evaluation involved scanning a fastcat phantom across a range of kilovoltage (kV) and megavoltage (MV) energies. The resulting Fastcat CT numbers were contrasted against reference values derived from the CT water phantom and the Fastcat phantom itself. Additionally, a CBCT simulation was executed using the Fastcat raw data and the CT scanner's software, with the generated images compared against those from the water phantom. The findings indicate that Fastcat CT scanner numbers closely align with reference values across both kV and MV spectra, with deviations remaining within 1%. Similarly, the CT scanner numbers and CBCT images produced via the Fastcat raw data matched reference values and images with high precision.

LIME has emerged as a leading method for explaining predictions from black-box models, yet it often generates inconsistent accounts for similar model inputs. This lack of reliability stems from the fact that LIME does not constrain the black-box model's explanations to remain stable across minor perturbations. This paper introduces S-LIME, a novel framework that resolves this limitation by integrating a stable LIME model with the black-box model to ensure consistent local explanations. S-LIME operates by minimizing the discrepancy between the black-box model and LIME within a local region, subject to a stability penalty. This approach yields two key benefits: first, it produces consistent explanations for similar instances, and second, it remains computationally efficient by solving a convex optimization problem. Empirical evaluations on real-world datasets demonstrate that S-LIME outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in generating consistent explanations.

This study introduces a novel categorization framework that leverages justification feedback to enhance performance. The system employs a hierarchical Bayesian architecture that incorporates user justification feedback as a specific feature, enabling the model to learn category structures and improve classification capabilities. The approach was evaluated on two datasets: a synthetic dataset and a real-world dataset comprising 1,000 flower images. In both cases, the model achieved superior performance compared to baseline methods.

The compound TbInO$_3$ is a promising candidate for a spin liquid, featuring a geometrically frustrated triangular lattice of isolated Tb$^{3+}$ ions. This study details the findings from inelastic neutron scattering measurements on polycrystalline TbInO$_3$, revealing that the magnetic excitations are well-modeled by a single-magnon spectrum derived from the crystal field Hamiltonian. The analysis yields a comprehensive set of parameters for the crystal field Hamiltonian and the exchange Hamiltonian, demonstrating that the system's energetics are dominated by the exchange interaction. Furthermore, the observed excitation spectra exhibit distinct vibronic structures, which are attributed to the excitation of local Tb$^{3+}$ phonons.

This paper demonstrates that the power-of-mean curvature evolution can be approached using both primal and Fenchel dual frameworks within a convex optimization setting. The evolution is modeled as an optimal control problem, where the convex nature of the functional arises from the smoothing effect of the heat equation. We derive a weak* form minimal norm solution to this problem and apply it to analyze mean curvature motion with quadratic growth. Additionally, we examine the mean curvature flow of convex sets to show that the quadratic-case solution corresponds to the Minkowski difference quotient between two such sets.

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have achieved remarkable success in image classification, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. This study investigates the frequency characteristics of CNN feature maps by examining the spectral properties of convolutional layers. We demonstrate that the convolutional kernels in CNNs can be effectively represented as a linear superposition of a few dominant frequencies. Leveraging this insight, we introduce Spectral CNN (SpecCNN), a novel architecture that learns a classifier directly in the frequency domain. By utilizing the Fast Fourier Transform, SpecCNN achieves competitive classification accuracy with standard spatial-domain CNNs while requiring fewer parameters and less computational time. Furthermore, we analyze the generalization capabilities of SpecCNN and confirm its efficacy through experiments on two image classification datasets.

This paper introduces a new approach to image grouping using deep neural networks, which has been demonstrated to outperform existing methods. The proposed framework, DeepCluE, utilizes a multi-layer architecture designed to determine the optimal number of image groups and their contents simultaneously. To achieve this, DeepCluE incorporates a specific loss function that encourages the network to classify new images into the same groups as their training counterparts. The effectiveness of this method was validated through experiments on the MS-COCO dataset, which confirmed significant improvements over current state-of-the-art techniques.

This paper outlines a system designed to detect organizational risks within corporate environments by leveraging automated news analysis, and it is built upon the premise that news articles often contain implicit references to internal company issues. The system employs a graph-based methodology to model the relationships between entities mentioned in news reports, utilizing graph analysis to identify risks that manifest across multiple articles. By combining this approach with natural language processing, the system automatically identifies risk-related entities and classifies them into specific risk categories. The authors demonstrate the system's effectiveness through a case study of a well-known data breach, followed by an evaluation of its performance on news articles from the 2018 D2D competition.

This study introduces a novel approach to classifying data by analyzing its topology. The methodology begins by constructing a simplicial complex from the input set, then applies persistent homology to identify topological features within the complex. These features are converted into a bar code representation, which serves as the basis for categorization using a specific distance metric. The resulting classification framework is designed to be both efficient and effective, as confirmed by comprehensive experimental evaluations.

Contrasimilarity stands as a novel binary relation that is both reflexive and transitive but not necessarily symmetric. This work introduces a game-theoretic framework to characterize contrasimilarities within directed graphs. We demonstrate that determining whether two nodes are contrasimilar corresponds to establishing that a specific set of vertices is reachable through a winning strategy in an associated game on the graph. Additionally, we explore how contrasimilarity relates to other binary connections and outline methods for computing its congruence lattices.

We provide a description of a 2-Lie group, denoted as $B\pi_1$, which serves as a higher-order generalization of a standard Lie group defined by a finite fundamental group $\pi_1$. This approach involves the string Lie 2-group, specifically the string group $G_\mathbb{R}$, which functions as a weak higher form of any simple, compact, simply connected Lie group characterized by its fundamental group $\pi_1$. We demonstrate that $B\pi_1$ is equivalent to the weak higher group $B(\mathbb{Z}_2, 2)$, alongside its associated classifying space $B^2\pi_1$. This study examines the generation of ion-acoustic rogue waves within a double pair plasma featuring non-extensive, bi-Maxwellian electrons and ions, and including both negative and positive ions. By applying the reductive perturbation technique, we derive the modified Korteweg-de Vries (mKdV) equation to model these solitary pulses. Our findings indicate that the amplitude and width of ion-acoustic rogue waves depend on the plasma's constituent species, specifically the plasma-to-ion mass ratio, the density of negative and positive ions, and the parameters of the non-extensive distribution.

The parametric decay instability (PDI) of Alfvén waves is a primary mechanism for converting wave energy into heat and particle acceleration in space plasmas. This study investigates the PDI within a laboratory-relevant plasma environment, specifically within a cylindrical plasma column. We utilize a hybrid kinetic-Maxwell code to simulate the process, modeling the system as a magnetized, collisionless plasma with a cold ion component and a kinetic electron component. The simulation begins with a cold plasma possessing a uniform magnetic field and a constant density, subject to an external driver that generates a transverse magnetic field aligned with the background field. This driver imposes a time-dependent sinusoidal oscillation on the magnetic field, which subsequently evolves into a turbulent state. The simulation tracks the resulting wave turbulence and its nonlinear interactions with plasma particles. We analyze the PDI by examining the temporal evolution of the Alfvén wave's magnetic field amplitude and the distribution functions of electrons and ions. Our results indicate that the PDI is triggered by the Alfvén wave's interaction with a specific subset of plasma particles, leading to a significant reduction in Alfvén wave amplitude. Furthermore, we observe that the PDI is accompanied by the excitation of lower-frequency magnetic field fluctuations and a substantial increase in the kinetic energy of the interacting particles.

This study examines the gravitational instability of thread-like molecular nebulae, accounting for ambipolar diffusion, by deriving a dispersion relation for density fluctuations. The analysis reveals that the critical mass and critical radius required for collapse are significantly lower than values predicted by models assuming a uniform density. Consequently, these findings offer a more accurate explanation for the mass and size distributions of observed molecular cores.

We investigate the quantum Zeno and anti-Zeno effects within the framework of the Jaynes-Cummings model, assuming a significant g-factor coupling regime. By employing a generalized master equation approach, we derive the reduced density matrix for a two-level atom, accounting for an arbitrary initial state of the field. Our analysis reveals that both phenomena are contingent upon the specific form of the spectral density, specifically the photon number distribution of the field. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a coherent state of the field uniquely ensures the robustness of these phenomena against variations in the spectral cutoff frequency.

This study examines the one-dimensional quantum spin-$1/2$ Heisenberg model with uniform Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions subjected to an asymmetric external field. By applying the Bethe ansatz, we derive the ground state energy and analyze the system's thermodynamic properties, specifically investigating the temperature dependence of the magnetization and internal energy. The findings demonstrate that both uniform exchange and Dzyaloshinsky-Moriya interactions can be thermally activated.

This paper introduces a distributed path planning algorithm designed for quadrotor swarms that ensures collision-free navigation through obstacles. The methodology employs a linear safe passage (LSP) approach, which utilizes a viability kernel to determine the set of safe states for each individual. By integrating these safe states with the constraints of the swarming formation, the trajectory planning problem is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP). The study also outlines an algorithm for computing the viability kernel and presents simulation results demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.

Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) has become a standard approach for addressing the domain gap between simulated and real-world data in computer vision. While current research predominantly focuses on adapting a single source domain to a single target domain, practical applications often involve transferring from a single simulated source to multiple, diverse real-world domains. This paper introduces CARLANE, a comprehensive benchmark comprising six real-world domains derived from the CARLA simulation. We evaluate various state-of-the-art UDA methods across these multi-target scenarios and present CARLANE-Net, a novel UDA architecture designed specifically for multi-target adaptation. Experimental results indicate that CARLANE-Net achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches in multi-target UDA tasks.

Hydrogels are extensively utilized in soft robotics, yet their surface roughness can significantly alter wettability, a factor that is frequently overlooked. This study investigates how dispersed particles within hydrogels influence their contact angles. We demonstrate that particles can effectively modulate these angles, thereby providing an additional mechanism to regulate soft robotic performance.

The shift to emergency remote teaching caused by the COVID-19 pandemic has prompted a reevaluation of online education, particularly regarding the need for a more student-centered approach. This study examines the relationship between engagement and academic achievement during the continuation of emergency remote teaching at a university in the United States. Using the Community of Inquiry (COI) framework, the research analyzes the correlation between COI dimensions and academic performance. Data were collected from 118 students enrolled in a blended course, employing the Community of Inquiry Questionnaire (ICOI-Q) to measure engagement and final course grades to measure achievement. Results indicate that cognitive engagement is the most significant predictor of academic success, followed by teaching and social engagement. These findings offer practical insights for both students and instructors aiming to enhance learning outcomes in emergency remote contexts.

This study introduces an autoregressive (AR) approach for analyzing radar backscatter to measure wind speeds at a high temporal resolution of 1 second. The method was evaluated using data from the L-band Doppler radar at the Southern California Valles Caldera, where 1-second intervals were compared against 10-second averages. Results indicate that AR analysis yields wind speeds with a mean error of 0.2 m/s and a standard deviation of 0.4 m/s, outperforming the 0.6 m/s mean error and 0.7 m/s standard deviation observed with 10-second averaging. Furthermore, the AR-derived wind speeds align well with anemometer readings, exhibiting a mean error of 0.3 m/s and a standard deviation of 0.3 m/s. These findings demonstrate that AR analysis significantly enhances the precision of L-band radar measurements for short-duration wind events.
