We examine the neutrino polarizability within the framework of the Standard Model augmented by right-handed neutrinos, contrasting our findings with existing estimates. Our analysis indicates that the tensor form factor is significantly larger than previously believed, while the scalar and vector form factors remain unchanged.

This study examines the emergence of rhythmic activity in a neuron-glial cell network. The model incorporates a conductance-based neuron-glial cell interaction, where ion exchange occurs between glial cells and neurons. This interaction is modeled using a dynamic equation for intracellular glial cell ion concentration. The dynamics of this system are analyzed through a mean field approach, demonstrating that rhythmic activity can arise from the coupling between glial cells and neurons.

We investigate the topological characteristics of a neutral spin-1/2 particle situated in a background magnetic field, where it undergoes Aharonov-Bohm phase shifts. This setup generates a non-trivial topological phase within the particle's internal spin space, resulting in a specific geometric structure for the associated spin Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that the geometric phase linked to this system corresponds to the solid angle defined by the spin vector on the Bloch sphere. Furthermore, we establish that the internal Hamiltonian's Berry curvature is proportional to this curvature density, linking it to the topological properties of the system. We also examine the thermodynamic implications of this geometric phase, showing how it influences the system's entropy and magnetization. Finally, we explore the connection between the geometric phase and the associated anyonic statistics, highlighting the role of the particle's internal degrees of freedom in determining its statistical behavior.

This study examines the dynamics of a diffusive particle in a bounded one-dimensional domain, where the boundaries are stochastic and subject to random fluctuations. We demonstrate that when these boundary perturbations are of a specific type, the particle's return time distribution exhibits a distinct non-monotonic behavior. Specifically, increasing the domain size can paradoxically shorten the mean first-passage time, while sufficiently strong noise can render the mean first-passage time independent of the initial condition. We attribute this phenomenon to a competition between two distinct mechanisms: the initial escape of the particle from its starting point and the subsequent exploration of the domain. We further show that this proposed mechanism is robust across various noise types and applies to both symmetric and asymmetric random walks.

This study introduces a new dataset comprising 1,000 endoscopy video frames annotated with surgical artifacts, serving as a benchmark for evaluating object detection performance in endoscopic scenes. The evaluation leverages this dataset to test a selection of pre-trained models, including YOLO, Faster R-CNN, and RetinaNet, alongside a newly developed architecture based on the Faster R-CNN framework. The proposed architecture employs a Faster R-CNN backbone, utilizes a ResNet-50 feature extractor, and implements a novel classification head designed to improve detection accuracy. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses existing pre-trained solutions in terms of mean average precision (mAP) and inference speed. Furthermore, the study examines the robustness of these detectors against occlusion and illumination variations, concluding that the proposed model exhibits superior resilience in identifying surgical artifacts within challenging endoscopic video conditions.

The proliferation of software development has led to a vast array of diverse and often cryptic identifiers for software artifacts, such as class, file, and package names. This paper investigates the origins, frameworks, and semantics of syntactic patterns found within these names. Through an analysis of the Java codebase, we identify and categorize 1,000 distinct patterns, then evaluate their respective merits and drawbacks. Our findings reveal that the most frequently used patterns are often of lesser quality compared to their alternatives. Furthermore, we observe that the development of new patterns is primarily driven by external influences, specifically the frameworks and languages employed during coding.

This work introduces a novel combinatorial framework for the Fock space associated with the vertex operator algebra $V_k(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, where $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. We establish a $q$-deformed square algebra structure on this space, thereby confirming a conjecture originally posited by the Cube group. Furthermore, we demonstrate a $q$-deformed bi-algebra isomorphism linking this Fock space to the basis of the $q$-Shuffle algebra introduced by Hahn-Wenzl. This mapping enables the derivation of a closed-form formula for the Macdonald-Mahler coefficients of the vacuum character of $V_k(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$.

This study examines the kinetics of grain development in duplex and triplex systems through a comprehensive analysis. By utilizing a comprehensive data-driven approach, we analyze the evolution of grain boundaries and grain sizes, revealing that grain growth in duplex systems is notably more complex than previously thought. Our findings indicate that the kinetics are governed by a combination of multiple mechanisms, with the specific dominant process varying across different length scales. Furthermore, we demonstrate that grain growth in triplex systems can be effectively described by a triple-power law, which offers a more precise description than models relying on just two power laws.

This study investigates the 3D estimation of human stance and form, focusing on the physical posture and shape of the human body. We present a new dataset comprising 3D human poses captured via motion capture systems, synchronized with RGB-D sequences from a single camera. This collection includes 3,000 distinct poses across 100 unique individuals, with each pose annotated by three different motion experts. We also introduce a novel human 3D stance estimation framework that integrates a 3D CNN for predicting joint positions with a transformer module for estimating body contours. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches in 3D human stance and form estimation.

The study focuses on a two-dimensional lattice where the density of electrons is low, resulting in a small number of electrons per unit cell. The model incorporates nearest-neighbor hopping and an interaction between electrons located on adjacent sites. The analysis examines the system's ground state and its excitation spectrum, alongside the examination of the anomalous Green's function and the superconducting gap function. The results indicate that superconductivity persists even in regimes where the gap function exhibits a sign change across different regions of the Fermi surface. Furthermore, the influence of the interaction strength on the system's properties is analyzed. The findings suggest that the system remains superconducting despite the presence of strong electron-electron attraction, which is consistent with the behavior predicted by the mean-field theory. The misalignment between the observed CKM matrix and the predicted one in light quark sectors poses a significant challenge for models of flavor. This study investigates how alignment within the framework of leptoquarks can resolve this issue. We demonstrate that, unlike in the Standard Model, the presence of a leptoquark allows for substantial deviations from alignment within the top-charm sector without contradicting current experimental constraints. Furthermore, we analyze the interplay between flavor alignment and flavor universality in this context.

This study introduces a novel machine intelligence framework grounded in category theory, specifically utilizing double categories to define the architecture of learning systems. We present a fresh methodology for modeling computational processes that captures both their internal computational steps and their interactions with external environments. Central to our approach is the representation of learning systems as collections of programs, where each program encapsulates the system's state, dynamics, and interaction capabilities. By employing the double category of spans, we establish a robust language for defining these programs and articulating relationships among learning systems. We demonstrate the utility of this framework by representing and combining diverse machine learning architectures, such as neural networks and reinforcement learning agents. Furthermore, we illustrate its potential in machine intelligence meta-learning by applying it to the task of learning to play Atari games.

This paper introduces a novel optimal sliding-mode control design for second-order dynamic systems. The approach employs a finite-time state estimator alongside a newly devised control algorithm capable of managing disturbances up to a specified bounded magnitude. The proposed control scheme is demonstrated to be optimal in the sense of minimizing the control effort required to steer the system state to zero at a designated terminal time. Furthermore, an algorithm for calculating this optimal endpoint control is developed, and its finite-time convergence is proven. The efficacy of the suggested controller is validated through simulations.

This study introduces a novel approach for quantitatively determining the inter-electrode spacing in lithium-ion batteries by utilizing low-frequency ultrasonic vibrations. The proposed method relies on the existence of a structured layering between the cathode and anode, which generates a mechanical resonance at specific frequencies. By measuring this resonance, the precise distance separating the electrodes can be derived. The technique was validated on two distinct cell types: a 2032 coin cell and a 4688 pouch cell. The findings demonstrate that this method is both effective and reliable, offering a significant advantage over conventional techniques by enabling non-destructive, non-contact measurement of the layered architecture.

This study introduces a levelness-based control strategy for the discrete-time linearized model of a gantry hoist, addressing the inherent oscillatory dynamics of such systems. The proposed controller employs linear state feedback to generate smooth sinusoidal trajectories, thereby eliminating the need for complex PID tuning. By utilizing a discrete-time linear model, the approach effectively mitigates the impact of sampling on the system's stability. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the stability of the closed-loop system for arbitrary sampling intervals and establishes the necessary and sufficient conditions for system stabilizability.

The task of image captioning involves generating textual descriptions for images, yet many existing models struggle with out-of-distribution data, such as noisy captions that do not accurately reflect the image content. This study addresses the challenge of mitigating such noisy data by introducing a collaborative distillation framework. This approach leverages a specialized "distillation" model designed to identify and discard inaccurate captions, while a "student" model learns from the remaining high-quality data to create descriptions. By integrating the distillation model's ability to filter noise, the student model achieves superior performance in handling unseen and noisy scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that this method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in mitigating noisy image caption data.

This study investigates sequences of subsets of the natural numbers, $\mathbb{N}$, utilizing sequences of ideals on $\mathbb{N}$ as a framework. We define a collection $\mathcal{A}$ of infinite sets with no finite intersections as a strong link to its components if the collection of all such intersections forms an ideal $\mathcal{I}$. We demonstrate that for any such strong link sequence, the collection of all sets in $\mathcal{A}$ with finite complement is also a strong link sequence. We provide a sufficient condition for $\mathcal{I}$ to be a proper ideal and show that this condition is equivalent to the requirement that the collection of all finite unions of sets in $\mathcal{A}$ has infinite cardinality. We also prove that the union of any family of strong link sequences is itself a strong link sequence. We further show that the dual of a strong link sequence is strong link, and that the strong link property is preserved under relativization. Finally, we derive several properties concerning the strong link sequences of filter bases and we define the concept of a strong link Fσalgebra.

We establish a framework for constructing arranged Ehresmann semigroups within universal classes of ordered algebraic structures. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the balanced product of a partial semigroup with a monoid forms a constructed arranged Ehremsmann semigroup. Additionally, we prove that any arranged Ehremsmann semigroup is isomorphic to the such constructed product, thereby extending the foundational Szendrei theorem.

This paper investigates the depth-to-width interaction within self-focus, a self-attention mechanism that employs depth hierarchies to manage self-attention across multiple levels. We demonstrate that increasing width significantly enhances model performance across various layers, a finding that remains consistent regardless of whether self-attention is applied at the token level or the sequence level. We further analyze the relationship between depth and width, proposing a depth-dependent optimal width that exceeds the standard constant parameter setting. Our experiments indicate that this optimal width grows with increased layer counts. To substantiate this, we introduce a theoretical framework based on the parallelism between self-attention and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs), which explains the accelerating growth of width requirements as depth increases.

This study details the synthesis of BiFeO$_3$ (BFO) nanoparticles using a sol-gel method at low temperatures, followed by characterization via XRD, FE-SEM, and UV-Vis spectroscopy. The resulting nanoparticles exhibited a hexagonal morphology with a particle size of 10 nm. Notably, the magnetization of these nanoparticles was significantly higher than that of bulk BFO, while the material demonstrated superior photocatalytic activity in degrading methylene blue (MB) dye and generating hydrogen. The enhanced photocatalytic performance is attributed to the high surface-to-volume ratio and the hexagonal structure, which facilitate rapid charge carrier separation. Furthermore, the material's favorable optical properties, specifically its wide band gap and high absorption coefficient, were identified as key drivers for its superior efficiency in both water splitting and dye degradation.

The Ca-K index, a standard metric for quantifying solar chromospheric activity, is derived from the 121.6 nm Ca II K line absorption profiles. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of long-term Ca-K index variations and their fluctuations using a 100-year dataset of equal-contrast images from the Kodaikanal Solar Observatory. This dataset, spanning from 1922 to 2019, was constructed by normalizing original images against their respective averages. Our findings reveal that the Ca-K index fluctuates significantly across all three temporal scales: long-term, medium-term, and short-term. Specifically, the index exhibits a prominent 11-year periodicity, with its amplitude peaking at approximately 0.12 during the 1990s and declining to 0.06 during the 1900s. Additionally, a 27-day cycle is identified, with the highest amplitudes occurring in the 1950s and 1980s. This periodicity aligns with the 22-year solar magnetic cycle, showing a phase shift of roughly 1.5 years relative to sunspot number maxima. The study presents the inaugural observation of the rare decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, utilizing $pp$ collision data with a center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV and an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector. A signal significance of 5.0 standard deviations is achieved, yielding a measured branching fraction of ${\cal{B}}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^+) = (3.1^{+1.1}_{-0.9}^{+1.0}_{-0.9}) \times 10^{-8}$ within the proton momentum range $0.5 < p_{\Sigma^+} < 0.7$ GeV/c. This result is consistent with the Standard Model prediction, which estimates the branching fraction at $(3.0^{+1.1}_{-0.9}) \times 10^{-8}$.

Symbolic execution is a widely used technique for generating coverage data and verifying software correctness, yet it is frequently hindered by infinite loop cycles and excessive branching, leading to a state explosion that hinders both scalability and feasibility. To address this, we introduce DST, a novel distributed symbolic analysis framework designed to enhance scalability and improve feasibility. DST leverages the concept of test depth to delineate the program's execution landscape into distinct segments, thereby isolating loops and branches within each segment. This isolation prevents loops from expanding indefinitely and reduces the branching factor encountered during analysis. Furthermore, we have developed a robust DST engine capable of handling complex systems, such as the Linux kernel. Our implementation demonstrates that the proposed approach significantly boosts both the scalability and feasibility of symbolic execution.

This study introduces a novel federated learning framework designed for collaborative training without a central server, leveraging one-sided trusted social networks. This approach enables nodes to exchange model parameters solely based on mutual trust, facilitating applications in domains where server infrastructure is absent or compromised. The proposed architecture supports a flexible, adaptive structure with variable levels of trust. To address the challenge of heterogeneous learning speeds among nodes, we developed a new algorithm that integrates both asynchronous updates and trust-based social relationships. This algorithm ensures that all nodes achieve convergence to the optimal model. Furthermore, theoretical analysis reveals that the convergence rate scales linearly with the number of active nodes, significantly outperforming traditional synchronous federated learning.

This study introduces a neural network architecture designed to classify brief English texts into two categories: spam and non-spam. The model integrates a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) component with a convolutional neural network (CNN). The LSTM captures dependencies across the entire sequence, while the CNN extracts local features from word embeddings. We evaluated the model using the 20 newsgroups dataset, achieving a peak accuracy of 90.0% and a mean average precision (MAP) of 0.413. The results demonstrate that the architecture effectively models text sequences and identifies salient features. Furthermore, the study highlights the impact of hyperparameter tuning on performance and confirms the superiority of the LSTM-CNN approach over standalone CNN or LSTM models.

Fabry-Pérot etalons are crucial components in various optical devices, including spectrometers, filters, and interferometers. This work derives the analytical expression for the transmission function of telecentric etalons, a configuration where the angle-dependent optical path difference is independent of the incident angle. This telecentricity is achieved by using a lens to focus the etalon, a design that enables the use of lenses with large numerical apertures without compromising performance. The analytical expression is validated through numerical simulations and experimental measurements. The resulting expression is applicable to the design and optimization of various telecentric etalon-based devices.

This paper examines the existence of multiple pairings within integer partitions that adhere to specific congruences. A partition is defined as having pairing elements when disjoint sub-partices can be identified within it that are both congruent to one another. We present a formula to calculate the total number of these congruent pairing elements in a partition, alongside a combinatorial interpretation of this formula. Our findings demonstrate that for any given congruence class, there exist partitions featuring such pairing elements. Furthermore, we establish a link between congruent pairing elements and ill-partitions, and we prove that any partition containing at least $2k$ parts can be decomposed into $k$ sets of mutually congruent sub-partices.

The increasing complexity of integrated circuits has driven a shift toward modular design paradigms, specifically the introduction of the chiplet model. This model enables the creation of advanced, heterogeneous systems by integrating smaller, specialized die into a single package, thereby enhancing design agility and reducing time-to-market. To streamline the development of these systems, the Codette framework was created. It offers a standardized methodology for defining chiplets and facilitates their interconnection using a unified, portable interface. This work outlines the framework's core capabilities and demonstrates their utility through a case study involving a heterogeneous architecture that combines a CPU, GPU, and AI accelerator.

Mixture cure models are frequently employed to analyze survival data from patients with chronic diseases, particularly those involving cancer. A significant limitation of this methodology is its reliance on stringent parametric assumptions, specifically the requirement that regression coefficients adhere to a normal distribution. This constraint often proves unrealistic when applied to data from clinical trials. To address this issue, we introduce a semiparametric extension of the mixture cure model that relaxes these strict parametric conditions. Furthermore, we develop a presmoothing strategy to mitigate bias arising from the smoothing process. The proposed method's efficacy is substantiated through a simulation study, followed by an application to data from a lung cancer trial.

This study examines the nonlocal measure dimension of graphs, demonstrating that this parameter is intrinsically linked to the spectral properties of the Laplacian matrix. We establish that nonlocal measure dimension corresponds to the critical exponent $s$ for which the fractional Laplacian $(-\Delta)^s$ possesses a well-defined integral. Furthermore, we identify nonlocal measure dimension as the unique exponent $s$ for which the Green's function of the fractional Laplacian exhibits a logarithmic singularity at zero. Finally, we establish the relationship between nonlocal measure dimension and the standard measure dimension within the framework of the local scale.

The rise of in-memory computing (IMC) has introduced a new class of hardware architectures designed to overcome the memory wall, which traditionally restricts computing performance by necessitating the movement of data between memory and processing units. These frameworks, which embed processing directly into memory, have become a focal point for next-generation hardware research. However, this architectural shift introduces novel security challenges, specifically regarding side-channel attacks that exploit data leakage during computation. This paper investigates such vulnerabilities by analyzing the PIM framework, which pairs a ReRAM-based memory array with a Processing-in-Memory Co-Processor (PIC). We present a novel side-channel attack that targets the PIM system's internal operations, demonstrating that the architecture leaks information through power consumption patterns during arithmetic and logic unit (ALU) computations. Our findings reveal that the PIM system is susceptible to a specific class of side-channel attacks, which we term "data-in-flight" attacks, which exploit the transient storage of data within the ALU. We further show that the attack can be mitigated by a countermeasure that involves the use of a masking technique to mask the data-in-flight attack. Our results highlight the need for a comprehensive security analysis of PIM systems to ensure their safe deployment in future computing environments.

We introduce a newly developed family of rational, closed-form polarization functions designed to describe rational and transition-metal species. Built upon a dipole-inspired model, these functions offer reduced computational expense and a more compact basis compared to traditional models, while maintaining high-quality performance. Specifically, for transition-metal species, this approach achieves an average mean absolute error of 0.16 a.u. regarding the electric field gradient tensor and 0.02 a.u. for the nuclear shielding tensor. Furthermore, the model accurately captures chemical trends, such as the variations in shielding and polarization tensors across different coordination numbers and oxidation states.

Seismic data is frequently compromised by localized noise, including blind spots caused by instrument failures, cable defects, or sensor malfunctions. While self-supervised deep learning methods have proven effective at restoring such missing information, their performance is constrained by the quantity of training data. This study introduces a transfer learning strategy designed to enhance self-supervised noise reduction. By training a primary model on abundant, uncontaminated seismic records and subsequently adapting it to scarce, noisy datasets, we achieve superior restoration outcomes. This approach not only mitigates the adverse effects of limited data but also enhances the generalization capabilities of the resulting models.

This study examines the connection between the charge asymmetry observed in the scattering of real photons during leptonic antilepton-proton reactions and the analogous charge asymmetry found in elastic lepton-antilepton-proton scattering caused by real photon emission. The analysis focuses on the role of strong interactions, specifically examining how they influence this asymmetry. The results indicate that, within the current precision limits of experimental data, strong interactions do not alter the charge asymmetry.

The spin-orbit-coupling Mott insulator Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ exhibits a complex electronic structure, yet its specific mechanism remains uncertain. This study utilizes scanning tunneling spectroscopy to examine the local density of states within an artificial Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ nanostructure. The resulting spectral data reveal a ladder-like pattern, which is interpreted as spin-polaron bands arising from electron-electron interactions. This interpretation is corroborated by a comparison with $t$-$J$ model calculations. The identification of spin-polaron bands in this material provides compelling evidence for the presence of Mott physics.

Causal mediation analysis seeks to identify how distinct causal pathways influence an outcome through specific intermediate variables. This study addresses a complex scenario where multiple mediators interact with one another and their effects are modulated by specific factors. We introduce a novel examination method utilizing the concept of multiply resilient interventions, which allows for the manipulation of multiple mediator variables simultaneously. This approach is particularly valuable for researchers aiming to determine the maximum potential impact of multi-faceted interventions. We outline the theoretical framework for this examination, define its identification criteria, and develop an estimation strategy. The method is applied to a dataset regarding the link between educational attainment and obesity, accounting for the mutual correlation between body mass index and waist circumference.

This Special Edition marks the culmination of a two-year, starshades-focused initiative led by the Starshade Project, an entity within the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's Exoplanet Exploration Program. The initiative aims to advance exoplanet research by equipping the global community with essential tools, data, and insights to support the upcoming launch of the first starshade. In that spirit, the Editor offers a brief overview of the two-year program and outlines the future trajectory of exoplanet research enabled by the starshades.

Suicide remains a prevalent issue in the digital age, with social media platforms serving as a primary venue for individuals to express their distress. This study introduces Robin, a new corpus comprising 1,000 English-language posts detailing suicide attempts or thoughts. Curated through the Twitter platform, the dataset features a diverse array of demographics, including varied ages, genders, ethnicities, and educational backgrounds, alongside self-identified mental health diagnoses. The collection encompasses both the initial disclosures of suicidal intent and the subsequent narratives describing the specific methods employed. Additionally, the dataset includes a specialized "control" group consisting of non-suicidal content. A thorough analysis of the corpus highlights its extensive size and rich linguistic variety, establishing it as a robust resource for advancing research into suicide prevention.

We introduce "superBlackian" mechanics as a novel framework for classical mechanics, a term coined by combining "super" and the negation implied in "blackian." This theory is defined by the absence of any black regions within its phase space. By utilizing the concept of "super"manifolds, we define a space wherein every point possesses tangent vectors, ensuring no point escapes coverage. We present a detailed analysis of "super"manifolds, followed by a construction of the "super"phase space as a "super"space derived from standard concepts of symplectic geometry. We establish the foundational principles of "super"classical mechanics, describing the "super"Hamiltonian flow and the "super"Hamiltonian equations. Finally, we apply this theory to "super"point particles, providing a concrete example of "super"mechanics.

This paper examines a second-order difference equation featuring a power parameter $\alpha$ that ranges between 0 and 2. We establish the global asymptotic stability of its zero equilibrium solution. Additionally, we derive the exact solution for the case where $\alpha=1$.

This study examines the group-invariant solutions of the Einstein field equations coupled with a nonlinear electrodynamics model that encompasses the Born-Infeld theory. The resulting metric is derived from a single free parameter, $f$, which is linked to the electric charge via $q = \sqrt{3}(1 - f)r_0^2$. The parameter $f$ is constrained within the range $0 \leq f \leq 1/3$. By analyzing the Kretschmann scalar, we demonstrate that the curvature singularity occurs at $r = r_0$. Furthermore, we establish the condition for the black hole horizon, $r_0 \leq 2M$, and show that the spacetime remains regular for all $f \neq 0$. The metric is valid for $f \leq 1/3$ and exhibits a curvature asymptotic to the Reissner-Nordström solution as $f \to 0$. Finally, we analyze the physical characteristics of the black hole, including its mass, charge, and temperature, and discuss the implications of these results.

This paper explores linear arrangements of $k$-dimensional subspaces within vector space structures. We demonstrate that within any such arrangement of $N$ subspaces, one can find a subspace containing at least $N^{k/p}$ of these $k$-dimensional subspaces. Here, $p$ represents the smallest prime number greater than $k$, and the bound is tight for the case of finite fields. We also derive a lower bound for the size of subsets of a vector space that contain no such subspaces. Additionally, we establish the existence of configurations with no $k$-dimensional subspaces, where the number of subspaces is exponential relative to the dimension of the space. These results are derived using a novel approach based on a new type of graph theory.

This study examines the scaling behavior of the magnetic susceptibility and geometric phase across the quantum phase transition in the 2D XY spin lattice at finite temperatures. We demonstrate that the magnetic susceptibility exhibits a critical scaling pattern, with its amplitude and critical exponent remaining consistent with those observed at zero temperature. Similarly, the geometric phase adheres to the finite temperature scaling hypothesis, confirming a zero-temperature phase transition of the 2D Ising model type via a universal critical exponent of $\nu=1$. Furthermore, we establish that the amplitude of the geometric phase scales with temperature according to a power law, indicating that its magnitude diminishes as thermal conditions rise.

We investigated the thermal phase transition of a two-dimensional Ising model using Monte Carlo simulations, specifically examining how the average spin flip time varies across different temperatures. Our findings indicate that average spin flip time increases with temperature, a result that contradicts the conventional view that hot systems evolve more rapidly toward equilibrium. To explain this, we proposed a model in which spin flip time is inversely proportional to the system's entropy, suggesting that higher entropy accelerates relaxation. We further hypothesized that spin flip time is directly proportional to the system's free energy, implying that lower free energy facilitates quicker relaxation. Both of these hypotheses were validated by our Monte Carlo data.

The proliferation of multilingual conversational agents has heightened the need for task-oriented dialogue systems capable of operating across diverse languages. This paper examines the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) in multilingual task-focused conversational agents, emphasizing the critical role of language translation. We demonstrate that integrating translation into the architecture of a multilingual system can substantially enhance performance. To achieve this, we introduce a translation-enhanced framework designed for task-oriented dialogues, which employs a single universal model across all supported languages. This approach utilizes an external translation module to convert queries and responses into a designated base language before processing them through the model. We evaluate this translation-augmented framework against a baseline universal model on the multilingual DialogLeaD dataset, covering English, French, German, and Spanish. Our results indicate that incorporating translation yields significant performance gains, with the most substantial improvements observed in French and German.

We introduce a novel method for analyzing short-term splicing regulation, utilizing RNA-seq data collected from a human neuronal cell line across multiple time points. Applying this approach to the neuronal gene *MAPK1* and the neuronal gene *RBM3*, we identified distinct regulatory patterns. While *MAPK1* exhibits a pattern consistent with immediate activation of pre-mRNA splicing machinery, *RBM3* displays a pattern indicative of the delayed activation of exon skipping mechanisms.

Data privacy is a critical concern for both individuals and organizations, with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) serving as a primary driver for its importance. Although numerous technical strategies exist to safeguard personal data, compliance with privacy principles remains a challenge for many practitioners. This study aims to deepen the understanding of how these strategies are implemented within the data privacy lifecycle. We conducted a qualitative investigation involving 12 practitioners, utilizing a specialized interview guide to gather insights. The findings reveal that practitioners possess a high level of awareness regarding data privacy principles and the associated technical strategies. However, the process of translating these principles into actionable technical solutions remains difficult, often requiring iterative development and refinement. Furthermore, the study highlights that adherence to these strategies is frequently contingent upon organizational context and specific project constraints.

We present an analysis of $n$-particle azimuthal angular distributions in $pA$ collisions, utilizing the McLerran-Venugopalan (MV) framework to derive the four-particle correlation function. This work extends the formalism previously established by the authors for two- and three-particle correlations. We demonstrate that the calculated four-particle correlation function in $pA$ systems aligns with the three-particle result in both the high-pT and low-pT regimes, thereby confirming the validity of event reweighting for three-particle correlations. Additionally, we examine the behavior of the four-particle correlation in the intermediate pT region and demonstrate that it exhibits a distinct pattern compared to the limits at high and low momentum transfer.

The formation of light nuclei in Au-Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=3$ GeV is investigated using a transport model that incorporates coalescence and recombination mechanisms. The study analyzes the influence of various nuclear sources on the resulting light nuclei yields. The findings indicate that light nuclei are produced through a mix of coalescence and recombination processes, with the dominant mechanism varying by nucleus type: protons and deuterons form primarily via coalescence, while $^3$He, $^4$He, and $^3$He are generated mainly through recombination. Furthermore, the resulting light nuclei exhibit a temperature of approximately 100 MeV, which aligns with the chiral magnetic wave temperature.

The study of exoplanetary atmospheres is a rapidly expanding field, with a primary focus on gas-dominated worlds. However, rocky planets may possess alternative atmospheric compositions, such as silicate clouds or vapor, which could alter their observable characteristics. This work examines the physical conditions of silicate cloud formation in the atmospheres of rocky exoplanets, specifically targeting the temperature and pressure ranges where these condensates are stable. We identify that the condensation zones for silicate minerals are highly sensitive to atmospheric pressure, with the equilibrium temperature for pure silicate clouds falling between 1,000 K and 1,500 K. We further analyze the implications of this finding for the atmospheres of rocky exoplanets, concluding that silicate clouds are most likely to form in the upper regions of hot terrestrial atmospheres. Finally, we discuss the potential for detecting these clouds through spectroscopic observations and highlight their significance for future exoplanet research.

This study examines the solubility of circulant graphs by analyzing their solvable Cayley representations. We demonstrate that if a circulant graph $C(n,S)$ is connected and its set $S$ does not contain $n/2$, then the corresponding croup generated by $C(n,S)$ is solvable provided $n$'s prime factorization includes at most one even exponent.

This study introduces an advanced method for computing the inverse of a matrix, leveraging iterative techniques that employ pre-conditioning and correction terms. These pre- and corrective components are derived from a generalized, low-order approximation of matrix inversion, which serves as the foundation for rapid iterative matrix inversion algorithms. The approach is particularly effective for matrices that are close to symmetric, a scenario frequently encountered in the solution of partial differential equations (PDEs). The method's versatility is demonstrated through its application to both linear and non-linear matrix problems.

This study examines the energy spectrum of primordial perturbations within the context of ultra-slow-roll (USR) inflation, incorporating back-reaction effects. Our analysis reveals that, unlike in the standard USR scenario, the inclusion of back-reaction causes the inflaton to transition from the USR phase to the slow-roll phase before the inflaton mass term becomes relevant. This shift occurs because the back-reaction of quantum fluctuations drives the effective potential towards a flat configuration, thereby inducing USR-like inflation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the inflaton mass term acts as the ultimate cause terminating the USR phase and triggering a transition toward slow-roll inflation. Our findings indicate that the resulting energy spectrum of primordial perturbations during back-reaction-influenced USR exhibits a nearly scale-invariant character.

The selection optimization problem (SOP) is a well-established challenge in combinatorial optimization. This paper introduces an enhanced variant of the problem, the enhanced selection optimization issue (ESOI), which aims to identify a subset of elements that maximizes the objective function while simultaneously ensuring the subset's size is as small as possible. We demonstrate that the enhanced version of several classic combinatorial problems—including the set covering problem (SCP), the 0-1 knapsack problem (OKP), and the 0-1 multiple knapsack problem (OMKP)—is NP-hard. Furthermore, we present a new algorithmic framework for solving SOPs, which is adaptable to various combinatorial challenges. This approach integrates a greedy selection strategy with a simulated annealing (SA) algorithm to optimize the objective function while minimizing element count. Additionally, we evaluate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to several classic combinatorial problems.

In survival analysis, researchers often investigate the probability of an event occurring within a specific time frame. While Kaplan-Meier curves are frequently used to estimate these probabilities, they can be difficult to interpret when dealing with extended time horizons. To address this limitation, we propose a new graphical method called "casebase," which offers a clearer alternative for visualizing event likelihoods over fixed-time windows. We demonstrate the utility of this approach through two empirical examples.

The recent surge in computing power has enabled the calculation of multi-loop Feynman integrals with varying dimensions, thereby significantly advancing theoretical predictions for LHC experiments. This overview surveys recent progress in computing multi-loop integrals, alongside an analysis of their impact on theoretical predictions. We also examine the physical significance of these results, supported by specific examples.

This study evaluates the performance of two object storage solutions, Apache Data Object Storage (DAOS) and Ceph, specifically within the context of scientific data retention. The assessment focuses on two critical scientific use cases: storing large-scale datasets and facilitating remote object access. To ensure a fair comparison, the analysis adheres to a controlled experimental methodology. The results indicate that both storage systems are viable for scientific data retention, yet they exhibit distinct performance characteristics. Specifically, Ceph demonstrates superior speed for storing large objects, whereas DAOS offers lower latency for remote access operations.

This paper introduces a virtual enrollment system designed to manage parking demand at public facilities, addressing the scarcity of available spots during peak times. The system leverages electric vehicle (EV) charging requests to optimize utilization of the growing network of EV charging stations. By integrating parking availability data with EV charging capabilities, the platform assigns parking slots virtually to EV users before they arrive. This approach ensures that EV vehicles occupy spots exclusively for charging purposes, thereby reducing the likelihood of abandoned vehicles obstructing parking areas. Furthermore, the study outlines a charging scheduling algorithm that incorporates parking reservations and EV battery state-of-charge data to enhance charging station efficiency.

Linearly self-dual codes (LCD codes) over finite fields are essential for modern data storage and transmission systems. This study investigates the existence and construction of such codes within finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$. We demonstrate that for any finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ and any pair of positive integers $n$ and $k$ satisfying $1 \le k \le n$, an LCD code of parameters $[n,k]$ exists. Furthermore, we present two novel methods for generating LCD MDS codes: the first constructs a $n \times n$ matrix to generate a code with parameters $[n,n-2,d_n]$, while the second produces a generator matrix corresponding to parameters $[n,n-2,d_{n-1}]$.

We demonstrate that a classical gravitational interaction emerges from a fundamental $U(1)$ symmetry operating on the complexification of a bundle containing loop-magnitude variables. This loop structure originates from the large-scale behavior of a quantum field theory. The resulting gravitational potential takes the form of a Fourier transform of a function derived from the potential's magnitude, which itself is a function of the holonomy around a closed loop.

Achieving a carbon-neutral future hinges on the large-scale adoption of renewable energy, yet this transition often incurs significant land-use costs. This study examines the trade-offs between electricity decarbonization and land consumption in the American West, a region where land availability is particularly constrained. We utilize a comprehensive dataset of 1.5 million land parcels, each annotated with its primary land use and potential energy output, to evaluate the impact of land allocation choices on decarbonization pathways. Our analysis reveals that shifting from coal to solar and wind power requires approximately 1.5 times more land than maintaining current generation mixes, while shifting to wind and solar bioenergy respectively requires 1.5 and 1.5 times more land than maintaining the current mix. We further demonstrate that prioritizing land efficiency for wind and solar bioenergy results in a significant increase in land requirements for decarbonization. We also show that accounting for land use conflicts can reduce the potential output of wind and solar bioenergy by up to 1.5. Cluster-randomized immunization trials are increasingly common, where the treatment is administered at the group level (clusters) rather than to individuals. While the primary objective is typically to determine the population-level impact of vaccination, this effect is obscured by the specific trial design, which randomizes groups instead of people. To address this, researchers employ per-protocol analysis to isolate the direct effect of vaccinating a specific individual. However, this approach is often impractical due to logistical challenges, such as the inability to vaccinate control participants in real-world settings. Consequently, there is a pressing need to develop a method that estimates the population-level effect using the available cluster-randomized data. This paper introduces a novel framework for such trials that employs inverse probability weighting to estimate the population-level effect from the data at hand.

The standardised Laplacian matrix, also referred to as the normalized Laplacian, is a fundamental tool in spectral graph theory. This study examines fractal Mobius octagonal networks, providing a comprehensive analysis of their standardised Laplacian spectrum. We derive explicit formulas for both the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors of this matrix. Furthermore, we utilize these findings to determine key graph-theoretical properties, including the fractal dimension, fractal Laplacian energy, and fractal Fiedler value, as well as establishing several corollaries.

This research examines distributed learning within a linear bandit framework characterized by distinct arms for each agent, where every arm is represented by a unique feature vector and label vector. The objective is for each agent to identify its optimal arm without exchanging these feature or feature vectors. We introduce a novel algorithm that enables a network of agents to learn their respective optimal arms through message passing among neighbors. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this proposed algorithm achieves a regret bound that converges to the same asymptotic limit as an idealized version in which agents share their feature and label vectors.

The growing digitization of healthcare records has created a significant demand for machine learning models capable of analyzing this data. However, current systems often lack the necessary data volume to train such models, necessitating the synthesis of new records. While existing methods typically focus on tabular data, the unstructured nature of clinical notes presents a unique challenge. This study addresses the task of generating synthetic text-based clinical records from a cystic fibrosis population using a Transformer-based generative model. The model was trained on the MIMIC-III dataset, which comprises de-identified data from over 60,000 admissions across multiple US hospitals. The research evaluates the generated notes against the original data across three dimensions: (1) linguistic quality, (2) fidelity to the original data, and (3) the model's ability to replicate specific clinical findings. The results demonstrate that the synthetic notes are both high-quality and clinically relevant, with the model successfully capturing specific cystic fibrosis-related features.

This study examines the $D^{0} \to K^{\mp}\pi^{+}\pi^{-}\pi^{-}$ and $D^{0} \to K^{+}\pi^{-}\pi^{-}\pi^{-}$ decay chains, which are mediated by a complex network of resonances. Utilizing data from the BESIII detector at the $e^{+}e^{-}$ collider BEPCII, with an integrated luminosity of $2.93\,\text{fb}^{-1}$, the analysis isolates the $K^{*}(892)^{+}$ and $K_{0}^{*}(1424)^{0}$ resonances. By fitting the invariant mass spectrum of the $K^{*}K_{0}^{0}$ system, the researchers identify a resonance at $1.84\,\text{GeV}/c^{2}$ with a mass uncertainty of $0.03\,\text{GeV}/c^{2}$ and a width uncertainty of $0.02\,\text{GeV}/c^{2}$. Additionally, the branching fraction for the $D^{0} \to K^{+}\pi^{-}\pi^{-}\pi^{-}$ decay is determined to be $(1.11 \pm 0.03 \pm 0.03) \times 10^{-3}$, where the first error is statistical and the second represents systematic uncertainty.

Novelpy is a Python library designed to evaluate the degree of novelty and disruptiveness within bibliometric and patent datasets by utilizing various metrics. It operates by first generating a matrix that calculates the distance or similarity between individual items based on selected indicators, and subsequently applying clustering algorithms to analyze this matrix. The library supports multiple types of bibliometric metadata, including citations, co-authorships, co-citations, shared keywords, co-occurrences, and titles. For patent data, it accommodates attributes such as assignee names, claims, dependent claims, dependent and independent claim sets, and co-patenting relationships. Users can select from several clustering techniques, including hierarchical clustering, k-means, and spectral clustering. The output provides both a visual representation of the clusters and quantitative statistics regarding their characteristics.

We introduce a method to achieve spatiotemporal modulation of a pulse's intensity by leveraging cross-phase modulation (XPM) within a birefringent crystal. This approach involves overlapping two optical beams: one acts as a "probe" carrying information, while the other serves as a "pump" to modulate the probe's phase. To demonstrate this, we used an 800 nm beam as the probe and a 400 nm beam as the pump to induce nonlinear refraction in a quartz crystal. Our results show that this configuration can effectively control the intensity profile of the 800 nm beam. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the 400 nm beam's transverse intensity profile is transferred to the 800 nm beam, confirming the method's potential for generating complex beam shapes. Finally, we illustrate that the 400 nm beam's temporal profile is faithfully imprinted onto the 800 nm beam, confirming the method's utility for advanced temporal shaping.

This paper presents the inaugural, to our knowledge, demonstration of an autonomous system capable of shooting recurve bows in competition, with the machine's performance evaluated against human archers. The system is built upon a modular framework that can be adapted to various shooting disciplines, such as archery, billiards, and table tennis. It integrates a specialized machine learning pipeline for object detection and trajectory forecasting, alongside a decision-making algorithm that leverages these predictions to determine optimal actions. The core control loop operates in a continuous cycle of perception, planning, and actuation, enabling the machine to execute full competitive rounds without human intervention.

In the context of online recommendation systems, the goal is to identify the most relevant items for a user. However, the user-item interaction data is typically sparse, which hinders the ability to generate precise recommendations. To address this, researchers have developed cross-domain recommendation strategies that leverage auxiliary data from related domains. Yet, existing methods often fail to effectively utilize the full potential of this cross-domain information. This paper introduces a dual-metric learning approach designed to enhance cross-domain recommendation capabilities. First, we employ a cross-domain metric learning strategy that trains a shared embedding space to align similar items across different domains. Second, we propose a cross-user metric learning strategy to refine the user-item interaction matrix by utilizing cross-domain user similarities. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, achieving significant improvements in both accuracy and efficiency.

This paper presents a characterization of the modal fragments of the Modal Mu-Calculus (MC), specifically those containing no more than one modal operator. We demonstrate that MC formulas with just one operator are equivalent to those in a new subclass of MC, known as the "segment class," which notably excludes the use of the least fixed point operator. We establish this by defining a new subclass of asynchronous, distributed automata called DDA, which is more powerful than previous models like the asynchronous automata of [1] and the distributed alternating automata of [2]. The segment class is precisely the class of languages recognized by these DDA.

This study examines the thermal behavior of two-dimensional intricate plasma layers, specifically focusing on the formation of hot spots and the onset of convection. The analysis reveals that the heat transfer mechanism is governed by the plasma layer's intricate geometry, which dictates the critical Rayleigh number required for convection. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that the temperature distribution within these layers is highly sensitive to their specific geometrical configuration.

This study examines the feasibility of recovering a source vector $x$ from an observed vector $y$, which is a linear combination of $x$ and $k$ unknown vectors $z_1, \dots, z_k$ within a given space. The vectors are corrupted by noise, and the matrices $A$ and $B_i$ linking them are derived from random Gaussian entries. We establish that when $k$ is constant, the probability of recovering $x$ approaches one as the dimensions of the vectors grow, provided the signal-to-noise ratio is sufficiently high.

This study introduces a deep learning approach designed to lower the X-ray radiation dose during cardio-angiography. The proposed method utilizes video interpolation to generate cardiac images at higher temporal resolution from a small set of low-resolution frames, thereby eliminating the need for frequent X-ray exposure. To achieve this, we developed a specialized deep learning framework that incorporates a novel loss function to ensure precise interpolation of the coronary arteries. We evaluated this technique on the public CASS dataset, which comprises 1,000 cardiac CT scans, and compared it against standard interpolation methods. The results demonstrate that our deep learning model significantly outperforms conventional approaches in terms of preserving artery details.

The Future Circular Collider (FCC) is a proposed facility designed to operate as a high-luminosity $e^+e^-$ machine, with potential upgrades to proton-proton collisions at significantly higher energies than current colliders. The FCC-e$^-$ is projected to deliver an unprecedented number of B-meson pairs, enabling the precision study of their properties and the investigation of rare decay processes. This capability will provide access to a vast array of novel phenomena, thereby expanding the reach of flavor physics. This overview outlines the FCC-e$^-$'s heavy-flavor production capabilities, its scientific objectives within the heavy-flavor sector, and the associated opportunities and challenges.

We investigate the neutrino barrier phenomenon within leptophilic $U(1)$ frameworks, where the vacuum energy density for the neutrino plasma is calculated. This analysis reveals that the barrier temperature is highly sensitive to the specific $U(1)$ extension, varying by factors of approximately 10 across different models. We also examine the impact of neutrino barrier formation on the thermal relic abundance of dark matter, specifically within the $U(1)_{L_\mu-L_\tau}$ framework. Our findings indicate that the barrier formation suppresses the relic density, a suppression that intensifies with higher neutrino masses.

This study examines the orbital dynamics of a hierarchical triple system comprising a supermassive black hole (SMBH) and a hierarchical binary consisting of a star and a black hole (BH). We investigate how secular interactions within this configuration can eject the stellar component as a hypervelocity star (HVS). Our analysis reveals that the SMBH's gravitational influence on the binary causes the binary's apsidal lines to precess, thereby altering the binary's eccentricity and periastron distance. These secular variations in eccentricity can trigger the gravitational wave (GW) merger of the binary pair. Such a merger leaves the surviving BH with a highly eccentric orbit around the SMBH, potentially resulting in the ejection of the BH and the companion star. We find that the probability of a binary undergoing secular eccentricity excitation and subsequent merger increases with the binary's mass ratio and the ratio of the binary's mass to the SMBH mass. Consequently, the likelihood of a binary BH being ejected as an HVS is significantly higher than that of a binary star. Our results indicate that the ejection rate of HVSs from the Galactic center is approximately 100 times greater than that of stellar velocity stars.

This study examines a class of singular stochastic differential equations (SDEs) characterized by drift coefficients that are merely measurable and Lebesgue integrable over time, coupled with multiplicative noise that is merely continuous in space. The analysis demonstrates that such systems exhibit feeble solutions, which are defined as the result of regularizing these disturbances.

We demonstrate that within models where $0^\# $ does not exist, the property of PFA implies that every nonstationary ideal on $\omega_2$ is either generated by the ideal or is a prime ideal. A parallel result holds for the nonstationary ideal defined on $P(\omega)/fin$.

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across numerous tasks, yet their application is frequently hindered by high computational costs and the need for extensive fine-tuning. To address these issues, we introduce "Adapter," a lightweight, modular framework that enables goal-oriented adaptation of LLMs. This approach utilizes a specialized structure to integrate task-specific knowledge into the model's final layers, allowing for efficient injection of task-specific information. By maintaining the core model's frozen weights, Adapters significantly reduce computational overhead and facilitate the rapid addition of new tasks. Furthermore, we develop a novel training strategy that leverages a goal-oriented mechanism to enhance the model's ability to handle diverse objectives. Extensive experiments across various downstream applications demonstrate that Adapters achieve state-of-the-art performance while drastically cutting down on both parameters and computational resources compared to traditional fine-tuning methods.

Traffic signs are essential for road safety, yet their recognition and categorization are critical for global applications. This study introduces the Mapillary Traffic Sign Collection, a dataset comprising 100,000 annotated images gathered from diverse global locations. The set includes 100 distinct sign classes, ranging from 100 to 1,000 examples per class. We report state-of-the-art results for both traffic sign classification and localization, alongside a novel approach to identifying categories from scratch. Additionally, we demonstrate how this dataset facilitates global sign categorization and outline its accessibility via the Mapillary platform.

Self-supervised learning has gained significant traction in recommendation systems, particularly for addressing cold-start issues. However, current methods often depend on auxiliary data, such as user-generated content or item metadata, which may not always be available. To overcome this limitation, we introduce SelfCF, a framework that leverages solely user-item interaction data. By framing recommendations as a cooperative effort between users and items, we develop a unified self-supervised model that integrates both user and item representations. Our approach employs a joint contrastive learning strategy to learn embeddings from both perspectives, thereby capturing the collaborative dynamics essential for accurate prediction. Comprehensive experiments across multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that SelfCF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, delivering substantial gains in Hit Rate@K and Mean Recalled@K. Furthermore, our analysis of the generated embeddings reveals that the framework effectively uncovers latent collaborative patterns.

We define generalized Tevelev divisors on moduli spaces of weighted rooted stable maps to $\mathbb{P}^1$ and establish a framework for their multiplicativity and vanishing. Our analysis extends Tevelev's original work, which focused on specific properties of standard Tevelev levels in moduli spaces of (unrooted) stable curves to generalized contexts involving curves with roots and weights. Our primary application involves a refined version of the cap product formula for these divisors, which is instrumental in computing the cohomology of moduli spaces of rooted curves. Furthermore, we derive a generalized form of the Atiyah-Bott fixed point formula applicable to the intersection of these divisors with boundary divisors.

This study presents a theoretical investigation of a gapped Dirac semimetal characterized by combined linear and parabolic dispersion relations. We demonstrate that the gap can be tuned from Dirac semimetal to insulator phases by adjusting the effective mass parameter. Additionally, we analyze the influence of the gap magnitude on the material's thermodynamic properties, including specific heat, entropy, and internal energy. Our results indicate that the specific heat exhibits a distinct T-linear regime at low temperatures, a feature attributed to the coexistence of linear and parabolic dispersion modes. Furthermore, we examine the Berry curvature and associated magnetoelectric response, observing that these quantities are suppressed in the presence of the gap. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings for the experimental realization of such a system within bilayer graphene.

Let $k$ be a perfect field of characteristic $p>0$, and let $X$ be a smooth projective curve over $k$ possessing semi-stable reduction with dual graph $G$. We establish that if $G$ is a tree and $X(k)$ contains at least one point, then for any $k$-place $v$ of a global field $K$ where $X(k_v)$ has a rational point, the geometric fundamental group of $X$ over $k_v$, denoted $\pi_1(X/K_{v,\text{ét}})$, is neither quasi-simple nor quasicentral. This finding extends the work of Eshteva and de Jong, who previously demonstrated the same result for local fields in equal characteristic $0$.

This study examines the detectability of high-order gravitational wave modes from compact binary inspirals using future detectors like Cosmic Explorer and the Einstein Telescope. We demonstrate that the third-generation of observatories will be capable of detecting these higher-order modes for a vast majority of massive black hole mergers, specifically those exceeding 100 solar masses. Furthermore, we analyze the detectability of these modes across the entire parameter space of the inspiral phase, showing that higher-order modes can significantly enhance the estimation of source parameters, including luminosity distance and sky localization.

The Gaia mission has identified numerous astrometric anomalies, including 1,000+ stars with proper motion residuals exceeding 100 mas, and 100+ with residuals surpassing 1,000 mas. These irregularities are frequently attributed to unseen companions, such as planets or brown dwarfs. This study examines the feasibility of detecting such bodies by analyzing partial orbital data from the first Gaia release. We simulated various astrometric signatures of companions with masses ranging from 10 to 1,000 Jupiter masses and orbital periods between 10 and 100 years, incorporating realistic noise models. Our results indicate that the Gaia mission can detect companions with masses greater than 100 Jupiter masses in orbits exceeding 100 years, provided the full orbital path is available. However, for partial orbits, detection is only possible if the observed arc spans more than 100 years, with the companion's mass needing to exceed 100 Jupiter masses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the astrometric residuals caused by these companions can be distinguished from intrinsic stellar variability, such as that seen in pulsating stars.

The 0/1 Knapsack problem is a well-known combinatorial challenge that has been widely addressed using Genetic Algorithms (GA). This study evaluates the performance of various GA strategies, specifically focusing on different crossover and selection methods, by analyzing their impact on solution convergence. Performance was measured using average fitness and average objective function values across 100 test instances. The analysis included three selection techniques—Roulette Wheel, Tournament, and Rank—combined with either one-point or uniform crossover. Results indicate that the Roulette Wheel selection technique yielded the most effective convergence for the tested scenarios.
